name: Tao Te Ching
info: The Tao Te Ching, or Laozi, is an ancient Chinese classic traditionally attributed to the sage Laozi and compiled during the Warring States period, the foundational text of Taoism and one of the most translated works in the world.

facts.made: Traditionally ascribed to Laozi, the "Old Master", whose historical existence is debated; most modern scholars hold it to be a compilation of sayings consolidated during the fourth century BCE
facts.form: A Classical Chinese text of around 5,162 to 5,450 characters in 81 brief chapters, in two parts, the Tao Ching (chapters 1–37) and the Te Ching (chapters 38–81); about three-quarters rhymed in Old Chinese
facts.where: Transmitted in the Yan Zun, Heshang Gong and Wang Bi editions; early manuscripts found at Dunhuang, Mawangdui and Guodian
facts.known: The Tao as the source of all existence; wu wei, "non-action"; simplicity and humility; paradox and the limits of language; avoiding war, harsh laws and heavy taxes; foundation of Taoism

t: Its author and date are debated: the oldest excavated fragments, the Guodian bamboo slips, date to around 300 BCE, and a relatively complete text probably existed by the mid third century BCE.
It describes the Tao as the root of all things and urges a return to harmony with it through wu wei, simplicity and humility, in laconic, paradoxical verse.
Central to philosophical and religious Taoism, it was reread by Legalists, Confucians and Chinese Buddhists, and is one of the most translated texts in world literature.
dyk: The two silk copies found at Mawangdui in 1973 put the Te Ching before the Tao Ching, reversing the traditional order, so one English translation of them is titled Te-Tao Ching.
ev: The Guodian bamboo slips, the oldest known version of the text, are written
The tomb at Mawangdui that held two nearly complete silk copies is dated to this year
The title Tao Te Ching, marking the work as a classic, is first applied under Emperor Jing of Han
Wang Bi writes the commentary behind the most verified of the received editions
Emperor Xuanzong of Tang declares himself an authority on the text, claiming descent from Laozi
John Chalmers publishes the first English translation
Archaeologists recover the Mawangdui Silk Texts
The Guodian Chu slips are found near Guodian in Jingmen, Hubei

sections.origins:
The Tao Te Ching, "Classic of the Way and its Virtue", is also known simply as the Laozi after its traditional author. Laozi, whose name means "Old Master", is a figure whose historical existence scholars debate. The first account of his life, in the Records of the Grand Historian by the Han historian Sima Qian, gives three stories: in one he is Li Er or Li Dan, an archivist and contemporary of Confucius who wrote a book in two parts at the request of Yinxi, keeper of a pass, before departing to the West.

Scholars give different dates. Alan Chan of the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy argues that archaeology indicates that bodies of sayings attributed to Laozi were committed to writing probably from the second half of the fifth century BCE, and that overlapping collections were consolidated during the fourth century BCE. No Western scholarship follows the traditional dating to the time of Confucius, and few now hold that none of the text predates the Zhuangzi.

The compound dao-de, "way and virtue", emerges only in the late Warring States period, and terms such as "ten thousand chariots" also point to a Warring States development or at least interpolation of parts of the text.
sections.content:
The text describes the Tao as the source and ideal of all existence: unseen but not transcendent, immensely powerful yet supremely humble, the root of all things. People, having desires and free will, often act unnaturally and upset its balance, and the work aims to lead readers back to a natural state in harmony with the Tao. It treats language and conventional wisdom as biased and artificial and uses paradox to sharpen the point.

Wu wei, literally "non-action", is a central idea, with meanings ranging from "not forcing" to "acting spontaneously". It explains ziran, harmony with the Tao, and sets simplicity and humility against selfish action; on a political level it means avoiding war, harsh laws and heavy taxes.

The modern text has 81 short chapters in two parts. The first, the Daojing, chapters 1–37, is often considered more metaphysical, and the second, the Dejing, chapters 38–81, more political. Unlike Confucian texts, its statements refer to no particular persons, times or places. The style is laconic, with few grammatical particles, and poetic, combining short declarative statements with deliberate contradictions that invite varied interpretations.
sections.making:
Most modern scholarship holds the text to be a compilation, as is typical of long early Chinese works. The Guodian slips of around 300 BCE contain only about 2,000 characters that correspond to it, divided only by section endings, and lack the last fifteen chapters, 67 to 81. Franklin Perkins argues that their absence is not coincidental and suggests that these chapters, with their support for punishment and lack of self-cultivation practices, were merged later.

Traditional sources report early versions of 64, 68 or 72 chapters. The Heshang Gong edition divided the text into its present 81 chapters and gave them titles, though this was not universally accepted until perhaps the Tang dynasty. Linguistic studies by William Baxter and Liu Xiaogan point to a date before the Chuci and, for at least a substantial portion, before the Inner Zhuangzi; Scott Cook's study of the Guodian texts supports this.

The title Tao Te Ching, which marked the work as a classic, was first applied under Emperor Jing of Han (157–141 BCE), though it appears not to have been widely used until near the end of the Han. The earliest versions were written in seal script, later ones in clerical and regular script.
sections.reception:
The late Warring States Xunzi gives the first reference to Lao Dan as a philosopher under the name Laozi, criticising him for having "insight into retreat and yielding, but no insight into firmness and trustworthiness." The Han Feizi contains the earliest known commentaries on the text. Its terms were reinterpreted by Legalist thinkers and Confucianists, and above all through Chinese Buddhism, which arrived long after the text was in wide use.

The three main transmitted editions are named after early commentaries: those of Yan Zun, of the legendary Heshang Gong, and of the Three Kingdoms philosopher Wang Bi (226–249). The Heshang Gong rose to prominence with Taoism under imperial patronage in the fifth and sixth centuries. In 719 Liu Zhiji argued for Wang Bi's superiority, but the Tang state kept the Heshang Gong in place because Wang Bi was less widely used. In 731 Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, whose house claimed descent from Laozi, declared himself an authority on it.

Readings changed over time: the Heshang Gong understood it largely through longevity practices, the Tang through Buddhist logic and the Song through internal alchemy.
sections.survival:
From the early Tang dynasty onward the text was transmitted mainly with the commentaries of Heshang Gong and Wang Bi. Song scholars compared old manuscripts to preserve what they took to be the older text, and later scholars such as Yao Nai and Ma Xulun continued to argue that Wang Bi's was the standard.

Archaeology has since recovered manuscripts older than any received text. In the 1920s and 1930s Marc Aurel Stein and others found thousands of scrolls in the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang, including more than 50 partial and complete manuscripts and a copy of the lost Xiang'er commentary. In 1973 the Mawangdui Silk Texts, from a tomb dated to 168 BCE, yielded two nearly complete copies, Text A and Text B, both placing the Te Ching first.

In 1993 the oldest known version was found on bamboo slips in a tomb near Guodian in Jingmen, Hubei: around 800 slips with over 13,000 characters. Both the Mawangdui and Guodian versions are generally consistent with the received texts apart from chapter order and graphic variants, and several recent translations draw on them.
sections.legacy:
The Tao Te Ching is regarded, with the Zhuangzi, as the foundational text of Taoism. It is central to both philosophical and religious Taoism and has been described as profoundly influential in Chinese culture, art and medicine more broadly.

First translated into French in the early nineteenth century, it is one of the most translated texts in world literature, next to the Bible: over 250 times into Western languages by one count, and 1930 translations into 94 languages by another. The first English version, by the Scottish missionary John Chalmers in 1868, drew heavily on Stanislas Julien's French; James Legge later translated it for the Sacred Books of the East. Chinese scholars and teachers including Lin Yutang, D. C. Lau, Wing-tsit Chan and Gia-Fu Feng produced English versions in the twentieth century.

Classical Chinese, with no tense, number or person and little punctuation, makes it hard to translate, and many passages seem deliberately ambiguous. Popular interpretive versions are disputed: Russell Kirkland calls them Orientalist fantasies, while Michael LaFargue and Jonathan Herman argue that they meet a real spiritual need in the West.

summary: The Tao Te Ching, traditionally ascribed to Laozi, is a short Classical Chinese text compiled from sayings during the Warring States period, known from bamboo slips of about 300 BCE. Teaching the Tao, wu wei and simplicity in paradoxical verse, it founded Taoism, shaped Chinese thought and has been translated more than almost any other book.
